title: Gregory v. Ashcroft
lead: Missouri judges facing retirement at seventy challenged the rule under federal age-discrimination law and equal protection. A majority found Congress had not clearly included appointed judges within the disputed statutory category, while seven Justices upheld the age classification as rational.

actors.name: Ellis Gregory and Anthony Nugent
actors.role: Appointed Missouri judges retained through yes-or-no elections

actors.name: Justice White
actors.role: Author of a separate statutory rationale joined by Stevens

proceedings: The district court dismissed both statutory and equal-protection claims, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court affirmed seven to two on June 20, 1991, with only five joining the plain-statement statutory reasoning.
limits: The Court did not exempt all state employees, decide Congress lacked power to enact clear coverage, overrule Garcia, or decide whether retention elections made these judges elected officials. The agency-deference discussion was divided and historical.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Appointments and retention elections led to mandatory retirement
paragraphs: Missouri’s constitution required judges other than municipal judges to retire at seventy. Ellis Gregory, an associate circuit judge, and Anthony Nugent, a court of appeals judge, had been appointed by the governor under the Non-Partisan Court Plan, then retained through unopposed yes-or-no elections. With two other judges, they sued Governor John Ashcroft in federal court, invoking the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, or ADEA, and the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.

The district court dismissed, finding them excluded as appointees on the policymaking level and finding a rational retirement classification. The Eighth Circuit affirmed. The Supreme Court reviewed both questions.

sections.title: Express coverage of states coexisted with public-official exceptions
paragraphs: The ADEA barred covered employers from discharging people at least forty because of age. Congress expressly included states and political subdivisions as employers in 1974, but the employee definition excluded elected officials, their selected personal staff, policymaking-level appointees, and immediate advisers on an office’s constitutional or legal powers. Ashcroft argued judges were policymakers or, alternatively, elected officials through retention voting.

The judges said adjudication applied law rather than made policy. They invoked noscitur a sociis, reading a word by its neighbors: policymakers appeared between personal staff and immediate advisers, suggesting a close working relationship with an elected official that independent judges lacked. Ashcroft emphasized common-law development, supervision of lower courts, procedural rulemaking, and bar regulation.

sections.title: O’Connor required a clear congressional choice to displace judicial qualifications
sections.cue: Explain the federalism method and its constitutional limits.
paragraphs: Justice O’Connor’s five-Justice statutory majority treated qualifications of important state officials as foundational to a state’s governmental identity. Divided authority fostered responsiveness, experimentation, and checks against abuse. Congress could override state choices within its powers, but uncertain language would not establish disruption of the usual constitutional balance; intent had to be unmistakably clear.

Sovereign-immunity and preemption plain-statement principles and political-function cases supported caution. Those latter cases applied less demanding equal-protection scrutiny to some citizenship qualifications for representative-government positions, recognizing significant state authority. They did not make state qualifications immune from the Fourteenth Amendment.

Garcia, the precedent leaving protection against Commerce Clause regulation mainly to national political processes, was not overruled. The majority viewed clear statement as assuring that Congress actually made the displacement choice through that process and potentially avoiding an unresolved constitutional question about qualifications.

sections.title: Ambiguity about policymaking level defeated coverage
sections.cue: Give the application without making explicit naming universal.
paragraphs: The phrase concerned appointees at a policymaking level, not whether judges made policy exactly like legislators or administrators. Discretion over publicly important matters could qualify. Although an unusual description for judges, it was at least ambiguous in a statute excluding most senior officials. The question was clear inclusion, not clear exclusion, and that ambiguity defeated the required statement.

The Act need not always name judges or every job: general coverage was clear where an employee unambiguously fell outside all exceptions. Here the plausible policymaking exception mattered. The Court left the retention-election alternative undecided.

It also considered possible Fourteenth Amendment section 5 authority. Earlier decisions had sustained the state-employer extension under commerce power while reserving section 5. Reconstruction expanded federal power, but political-function precedents and Pennhurst’s caution against inferring an unstated section 5 purpose reinforced the same conclusion under either possible source. The Court did not decide Congress was powerless to provide unmistakable coverage.

sections.title: Seven Justices found rational reasons for the age rule
paragraphs: Age was not suspect and no fundamental right to judicial office was asserted, so rational-basis review applied. Missouri could seek competence, avoid repeated difficult individualized aging assessments, create orderly opportunities for other qualified judges, and use predictable retirement arrangements.

The Court did not find every or most judges incapable at seventy. A general line could address deterioration risk, and voluntary retirement or impeachment might be insufficient. Long terms, limited public visibility, and infrequent unopposed retention votes provided less accountability than ordinary elections. Other employees’ shortcomings could be observed and addressed more readily. Those differences rationally explained the age boundary and distinct treatment despite imperfect generalization.

sections.title: White reached the same result through ordinary interpretation
sections.cue: Distinguish his rationale and agency position.
paragraphs: Justice White, joined by Stevens, rejected the added clear-statement requirement because Congress had already expressly covered states. Importance to a state could not overcome a valid federal conflict. He found the rule inconsistent with Garcia, unsupported by alienage cases, uncertain in scope, burdensome in demanding lists, and especially inappropriate for section 5 legislation meant to overcome sovereignty.

He nevertheless considered judges policymakers under ordinary interpretation: common-law decisions selected alternatives and shaped future rules at a high official level. The exceptions shared a connection to elected officials, not necessarily close working relations; requiring closeness would make the policymaking category redundant. Identical Title VII language and legislative history supported a distinct category including judges.

White also rejected deference to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, characterizing its contrary view as a litigation position inconsistent with text. He disputed that an administrative ruling established the proposed close-relationship restriction. That analysis was his separate position, not a Court holding on the agency.

sections.title: Blackmun would apply the statute to the judges
sections.cue: State the dissent and exact alignment.
paragraphs: Justice Blackmun, joined by Marshall, agreed with White’s criticism of clear statement but read the exception differently. Neighboring personal-staff and adviser language indicated cabinet-like policymakers close to the appointing official, unlike independent judges. Amendment history and a conference instruction for narrow construction supported that view; isolated comments about judges did not overcome it.

Alternatively, under then-governing Chevron doctrine he would defer to the Commission’s reasonable consistent interpretation, supported in his view by administrative adjudication and enforcement history rather than convenience in litigation. He would invalidate retirement under the ADEA and did not reach equal protection.

On June 20, 1991, the Court affirmed seven to two. Rehnquist, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter joined O’Connor fully; White and Stevens joined the factual and equal-protection portions and judgment. Blackmun and Marshall dissented. The result concerned these appointed judges and this statute, not exclusion of every state employee.
